[{:db/id 17592186166880 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c7df86f0-3809-56f0-adcd-fb286616dfa3" "question-3f3b4139-4781-5e1e-8511-61fe405f4cab" "question-5213d5bf-5843-5c8c-8790-014b534c60aa" "question-75809447-c869-5206-aa76-8147e22ce3d8" "question-b743d271-bfde-5d80-a2b4-b7cbdaa6f1f5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166485 :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\widetilde{\mathbf n},$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle x,\: 2z,\: z-y \right\rangle\!, 
\quad 
\widetilde{\mathbf{n}}(x,y,z) = \left\langle z,\: -y,\: -x \right\rangle\!,
\quad
\mathbf n = \dfrac{\widetilde{\mathbf{n}}}{\Vert \widetilde{\mathbf{n}} \Vert}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

![](images/41/4152d997be216db1a67b5f55ee112d1008ea7399e57f699ac62ba03654bd7fd5.svg)

what is the missing expression?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166881 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e4c6d18b-d618-53cd-9fce-a599b57a0c5a" "question-6480541e-888b-58cb-a4eb-1a531ae87114"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166882 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-49459c91-bfac-5582-aa3d-bc1bfea60a7b" "question-aa928e5a-70af-5b00-a980-606761f10bda" 17592186167131 "question-2f0f5aff-a329-55d0-a382-ebd7a7992774"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c7df86f0-3809-56f0-adcd-fb286616dfa3" :question/id #uuid "c7df86f0-3809-56f0-adcd-fb286616dfa3" :question/math-academy-id "q-161204" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\overset{~}{n},$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,xy,\,{y}^{2}-1⟩\,,\,\overset{~}{n}(x,y,z)=⟨{y}^{2},\,2x,\,-z⟩\,,\,n=\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}\frac{2{x}^{2}y+z}{\boxed{}}\,\text{d}S
$$

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨{y}^{2},\,2x,\,-z⟩}{\sqrt{{({y}^{2})}^{2}+(2x)^{2}+(-z)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨{y}^{2},\,2x,\,-z⟩}{\sqrt{{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨{y}^{2},\,2x,\,-z⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,xy,\,{y}^{2}-1⟩\cdot \frac{⟨{y}^{2},\,2x,\,-z⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,xy,\,{y}^{2}-1⟩\cdot ⟨{y}^{2},\,2x,\,-z⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}z+2{x}^{2}y-z({y}^{2}-1)}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}y+z}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}y+z}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2190c13e-d51f-542e-bd67-2b30e8f5c940"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$

$$

$$

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}\frac{\boxed{}}{\sqrt{9{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2z,\,y,\,3{x}^{2}⟩}{\sqrt{(2z)^{2}+(y)^{2}+{(3{x}^{2})}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨2z,\,y,\,3{x}^{2}⟩}{\sqrt{4{z}^{2}+{y}^{2}+9{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨2z,\,y,\,3{x}^{2}⟩}{\sqrt{9{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,-z,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{⟨2z,\,y,\,3{x}^{2}⟩}{\sqrt{9{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨y,\,-z,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨2z,\,y,\,3{x}^{2}⟩}{\sqrt{9{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2yz-yz+3{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{9{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+yz}{\sqrt{9{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}

$F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=1$ for  $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =1\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163846 :answer-field/correct 17592186163848 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-e4c6d18b-d618-53cd-9fce-a599b57a0c5a" :question/id #uuid "e4c6d18b-d618-53cd-9fce-a599b57a0c5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161186" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$

For the surface $z=2$ for  $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x+y.\end{aligned}

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\,y+\frac{1}{2}\,{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}

$F(x,y,z)=⟨z+x,\,x+y,\,2x+6⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=-x+2y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=2\sqrt{3}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=-x+2y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=-x+2y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+x,\,x+y,\,2x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨2y,\,x+y,\,2x+6⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2y-2(x+y)+2x+6) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot 2\sqrt{3} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-27f85e1d-9f83-541a-b342-23041c17ed8f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id *Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\frac{3}{2}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$

$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-\frac{y}{2}+3$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,\frac{1}{2},\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=3,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-3.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,2y,\,2z-x-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,2y,\,(2x-y+6)-x-y⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,2y,\,x-2y+6⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2x-2y-2(x-2y+6)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2y-12).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{3}(2y-12)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{3}(2y-12)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{3}(2y-12)\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{3}}(2y-12)\cdot \frac{\cancel{3}}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-6)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(y-6)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}(y-6)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[x]_{0}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-6y]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2\cdot (-12) \\  & =-24\end{aligned}

17592186167131 :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,z+3⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x+y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{3}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z+3⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x,\,y,\,x+y+3⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-x-y+(x+y+3)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163864 :answer-field/correct 17592186163869 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-2f0f5aff-a329-55d0-a382-ebd7a7992774" :question/id #uuid "2f0f5aff-a329-55d0-a382-ebd7a7992774" :question/math-academy-id "q-162548" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,x+1,\,-y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x-4y+1$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 4.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=3\sqrt{2}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-4y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,4,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-4y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,x+1,\,-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨x-4y+1,\,x+1,\,-y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}(x-4y+1-4(x+1)+y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}(-3x-3y-3) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\cdot 3\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{2}}}(-x-y-1)\cdot 3\cancel{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}(x+y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+xy+x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}(2y+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3[{y}^{2}+4y]_{0}^{4} \\  & =-3\cdot 32 \\  & =-96\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7f22f763-7742-563a-8020-3b6c5519f8c8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7f22f763-7742-563a-8020-3b6c5519f8c8" :answer-field/id #uuid "7f22f763-7742-563a-8020-3b6c5519f8c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-974560cd-4e8d-59bd-8077-c163da225937" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3cae5a31-54ec-52d7-9829-e6f79d0db7b0" "answer-228c1e6f-6068-550e-b050-12aa6caa4351" "answer-974560cd-4e8d-59bd-8077-c163da225937" "answer-52b6e1b8-f74d-549f-80b2-b5dec0190106" "answer-03158da1-b1d2-5e08-9fb3-bcf52d0b7ade"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3cae5a31-54ec-52d7-9829-e6f79d0db7b0" :answer/id #uuid "3cae5a31-54ec-52d7-9829-e6f79d0db7b0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-228c1e6f-6068-550e-b050-12aa6caa4351" :answer/id #uuid "228c1e6f-6068-550e-b050-12aa6caa4351" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-48" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-974560cd-4e8d-59bd-8077-c163da225937" :answer/id #uuid "974560cd-4e8d-59bd-8077-c163da225937" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-96" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52b6e1b8-f74d-549f-80b2-b5dec0190106" :answer/id #uuid "52b6e1b8-f74d-549f-80b2-b5dec0190106" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-03158da1-b1d2-5e08-9fb3-bcf52d0b7ade" :answer/id #uuid "03158da1-b1d2-5e08-9fb3-bcf52d0b7ade" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "96" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167130 :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+2y-2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=3.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x+2y-2$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-2,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=2.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y-2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,y,\,2x+2y-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2x+2y-(2x+2y-2)) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2}{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\cancel{3}}\cdot \cancel{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot 3\cdot 2 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163858 :answer-field/correct 17592186163863 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

 

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter. 

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166981 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{3y-z}{5}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}3y-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\cdot 3\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{2}}}(-x-y-1)\cdot 3\cancel{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}(x+y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+xy+x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}(2y+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3[{y}^{2}+4y]_{0}^{4} \\  & =-3\cdot 32 \\  & =-96\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7f22f763-7742-563a-8020-3b6c5519f8c8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7f22f763-7742-563a-8020-3b6c5519f8c8" :answer-field/id #uuid "7f22f763-7742-563a-8020-3b6c5519f8c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-974560cd-4e8d-59bd-8077-c163da225937" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3cae5a31-54ec-52d7-9829-e6f79d0db7b0" "answer-228c1e6f-6068-550e-b050-12aa6caa4351" "answer-974560cd-4e8d-59bd-8077-c163da225937" "answer-52b6e1b8-f74d-549f-80b2-b5dec0190106" "answer-03158da1-b1d2-5e08-9fb3-bcf52d0b7ade"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3cae5a31-54ec-52d7-9829-e6f79d0db7b0" :answer/id #uuid "3cae5a31-54ec-52d7-9829-e6f79d0db7b0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-228c1e6f-6068-550e-b050-12aa6caa4351" :answer/id #uuid "228c1e6f-6068-550e-b050-12aa6caa4351" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-48" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-974560cd-4e8d-59bd-8077-c163da225937" :answer/id #uuid "974560cd-4e8d-59bd-8077-c163da225937" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-96" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52b6e1b8-f74d-549f-80b2-b5dec0190106" :answer/id #uuid "52b6e1b8-f74d-549f-80b2-b5dec0190106" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-03158da1-b1d2-5e08-9fb3-bcf52d0b7ade" :answer/id #uuid "03158da1-b1d2-5e08-9fb3-bcf52d0b7ade" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "96" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167130 :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+2y-2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=3.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x+2y-2$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-2,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=2.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y-2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,y,\,2x+2y-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2x+2y-(2x+2y-2)) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2}{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\cancel{3}}\cdot \cancel{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot 3\cdot 2 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163858 :answer-field/correct 17592186163863 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

 

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter. 

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,xy,\,{y}^{2}-1⟩\cdot \frac{⟨{y}^{2},\,2x,\,-z⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,xy,\,{y}^{2}-1⟩\cdot ⟨{y}^{2},\,2x,\,-z⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}z+2{x}^{2}y-z({y}^{2}-1)}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}y+z}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}y+z}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{4}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{(-3z)^{2}+(x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{9{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨{x}^{2},\,2xz,\,x+y⟩\cdot \frac{⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨{x}^{2},\,2xz,\,x+y⟩\cdot ⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{2}z+2{x}^{2}z+2y(x+y)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2xy+2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{2xy+2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5213d5bf-5843-5c8c-8790-014b534c60aa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-662e48f4-a2f4-58ca-946c-9c7fd0f8d49d" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z+x,\,x+y,\,2x+6⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=-x+2y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=2\sqrt{3}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=-x+2y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=-x+2y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+x,\,x+y,\,2x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨2y,\,x+y,\,2x+6⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2y-2(x+y)+2x+6) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot 2\sqrt{3} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-49459c91-bfac-5582-aa3d-bc1bfea60a7b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-27f85e1d-9f83-541a-b342-23041c17ed8f" :answer-field/id #uuid *Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=3\sqrt{2}.$*"] ["question-2f0f5aff-a329-55d0-a382-ebd7a7992774" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.

Notice that our surface $z=x-4y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,4,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-4y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,x+1,\,-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨x-4y+1,\,x+1,\,-y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}(x-4y+1-4(x+1)+y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}(-3x-3y-3) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1)\cdot 3\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{2}}}(-x-y-1)\cdot 3\cancel{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}(x+y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+xy+x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{4}(2y+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3[{y}^{2}+4y]_{0}^{4} \\  & =-3\cdot 32 \\  & =-96\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2f0f5aff-a329-55d0-a382-ebd7a7992774" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-7f22f763-7742-563a-8020-3b6c5519f8c8" :answer-field/id #uuid $$"] [17592186167130 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] [17592186163858 :answer-field/correct 17592186163863] [17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces."] [17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign."] [17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter.

So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces."] [17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign.

As in the case of two-dimensional vector fields, we have a choice between two possible normal vectors at each point. For instance, we could have picked the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction, as shown below.

<div id="graphic-b46ee2d2f4637027c6704e244e0b2f96" class="graphic"><img src="/graphics/b46ee2d2f4637027c6704e244e0b2f96" /></div> 

The key takeaway is that when calculating the flux of a vector field across a surface, we must be clear about which orientation we're measuring our flux relative to."] [17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter. 

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we have that

\begin{align*}
\mathbf r_x =  \langle 1, 0, 0\rangle = \mathbf i, \qquad \mathbf r_y =  \langle 0, 1, 0\rangle = \mathbf j.
\end{align*}

So, the fundamental vector product is given by

\[
\mathbf r_x \times\mathbf r_y = \mathbf i\times\mathbf j = \mathbf k
\]

and therefore

\[
|| \mathbf r_x \times\mathbf r_y|| = ||\mathbf k|| =1. 
\]

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. Let's see an example."]]}

:question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\widetilde{\mathbf n},$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle x,\: 2z,\: z-y \right\rangle\!, 
\quad 
\widetilde{\mathbf{n}}(x,y,z) = \left\langle z,\: -y,\: -x \right\rangle\!,
\quad
\mathbf n = \dfrac{\widetilde{\mathbf{n}}}{\Vert \widetilde{\mathbf{n}} \Vert}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

![](images/35/35bcfa2242051bed034ac3343c1a6d67f94916d4267030f726e2bd27cbbe02f1.png)

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\widetilde{\mathbf n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{(z)^{2}+(-y)^{2}+(-x)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{z}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,2z,\,z-y⟩\cdot \frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨x,\,2z,\,z-y⟩\cdot ⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{xz-2yz-x(z-y)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{xy-2yz}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{xy-2yz}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048376} {:db/id 17592186167126 :question/id #uuid "7492e5fe-6cc9-5d4b-8d1f-20d212147cee" :question/math-academy-id "q-160838"} {:db/id 17592186167127 :question/id #uuid Through a Horizontal Plane"}] :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle z,\: z,\: 4xy\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=1$ for $0\leq x\leq 1$ and $0\leq y\leq 1.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=1$ for  $0\leq x\leq 1$ and $0\leq y\leq 1,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
\mathbf n = \langle 0,\, 0,\, -1\rangle.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,z,\,4xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,4xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$

$$

Through a Tilted Plane"}] :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle y,\: 0,\: z\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+2y$ for $0\leq *Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| =3.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = 0, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,0,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨y,\,0,\,2x+2y⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2y+0x+2x+2y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2x) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2}{3}x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}x\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}x\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\cancel{3}}x\cdot \cancel{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[y]_{0}^{1}\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 4 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167129 :question/id #uuid "018ba806-567b-5332-8cf5-cb28969716b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-161158"} {:db/id 17592186167130 :question/id #uuid "07582355-f319-5419-a760-27151ce99dcb" :question/math-academy-id "q-161244" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166882 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9a62365-4278-557f-ba76-caa31abe7869" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a50551bb-2bfa-545f-bfec-d2070d12162f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186163859} {:answer/id #uuid "ae6f0a12-f232-5e2b-b2f1-2e7b023264fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186163860} {:answer/id #uuid "bb1dbc88-e2c8-53cd-823e-c82d725a89d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186163861} {:answer/id #uuid "fd394791-056b-5b7b-b1af-f84d65cc9169" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186163862} {:answer/id #uuid "0d264df1-7f0b-5421-8eb3-0926a18534a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186163863}] :answer-field/id #uuid "2ab8ce14-f8c3-5bfc-a6f7-64b0895b0b67" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186163858}] :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x, y, z) = ⟨x, y, z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z = 2x + 2y - 2$ for $0 \le x \le 3$ and $-1 \le y \le 1$. "34eb87b9-7036-55c0-88eb-1b1efbd11584" :topic/math-academy-id 3178} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167782 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168144 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle xz + y,\: x^2,\: 2y-z^2 \right\rangle\!, 
\qquad 
\mathbf{n}(x,y,z) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\left\langle 2,\: 0,\: -1 \right\rangle\!.
$$

Let's construct a surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}.$

First, we recall that if $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}((xz+y)\cdot 2+{x}^{2}\cdot 0+(2y-{z}^{2})\cdot (-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2xz+2y-2y+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf n$ can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{∬}_{S}2xz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S\end{aligned}
$$

We can then evaluate this integral using the usual methods." :tutorial/id #uuid "c936101d-fbb9-594d-888c-2327d0908e71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7632 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid Through a Horizontal Plane"} :step/id #uuid "53d98073-01e7-5129-ad66-75d01c7d3e9d" :step/math-academy-id 657083 :step/next {:db/id 17592186362446}} {:db/id 17592186167785 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168145 :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s.
$$

The flux measures the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ as depicted below.

![](images/23/2392d6c27fc6767c78172936d6df37b3dfec8b2198abbdf9e22b87d4337ed9da.png)

Flux is always measured with respect to a preselected unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and we have two choices of orientation for this vector. If we measure the flux relative to the unit normal pointing in the *opposite* direction, our flux will have the *same* magnitude but *opposite* sign.

![](images/e4/e451548a5d9874b9eff9d61c2d423696dc76a3f560e2936eb7bdb3a9cbfbed49.png)

This lesson aims to extend the concept of flux to three-dimensional vector fields. But first, we need a brief discussion on surface orientations." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a17f47e-f50d-578f-a41c-9e537ded3620" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7725 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "507e9c0b-b2be-5bf9-a53c-e763d7e4315b" :step/math-academy-id 657075 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167787}} {:db/id 17592186167786 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign.

As in the case of two-dimensional vector fields, we have a choice between two possible normal vectors at each point. For instance, we could have picked the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction, as shown below.

<div id="graphic-b46ee2d2f4637027c6704e244e0b2f96" class="graphic"><img src="/graphics/b46ee2d2f4637027c6704e244e0b2f96" /></div> 

The key takeaway is that when calculating the flux of a vector field across a surface, we must be clear about which orientation we're measuring our flux relative to." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "4b9873f3-a548-5ea9-a86b-7682d0efa06b" :step/math-academy-id 657077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167782}} {:db/id 17592186167787 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "15c5dca7-7c90-57e5-be91-60bf5e44e76b" :step/math-academy-id 657076 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167786}} {:db/id 17592186167788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166882 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166487 :question/id #uuid "35c3c9ba-60b0-5bcf-8e9c-2862ece44e7e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12454"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9a62365-4278-557f-ba76-caa31abe7869" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167129} {:db/id 17592186167130} {:db/id 17592186278417} {:db/id 17592186278418} {:db/id 17592186281387} {:db/id 17592186281388} {:db/id 17592186281492} {:db/id 17592186281494} {:db/id 17592186281496} {:db/id 17592186369894} {:db/id 17592186369908}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "99f84857-19d8-532f-b1f8-974d1ed142df" :step/math-academy-id 657087} {:db/id 17592186167789 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter. 

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we have that

\begin{align*}
\mathbf r_x =  \langle 1, 0, 0\rangle = \mathbf i, \qquad \mathbf r_y =  \langle 0, 1, 0\rangle = \mathbf j.
\end{align*}

So, the fundamental vector product is given by

\[
\mathbf r_x \times\mathbf r_y = \mathbf i\times\mathbf j = \mathbf k
\]

and therefore

\[
|| \mathbf r_x \times\mathbf r_y|| = ||\mathbf k|| =1. 
\]

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3a45ce20-02a0-56e8-9b38-add2ba9480d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7733 :tutorial/title "The Fundamental Vector Product for a Horizontal Plane"} :step/id #uuid "e8905e0e-c7f6-5708-9e74-d2d69c659271" :step/math-academy-id 657082 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167784}} {:db/id 17592186362446 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362413 :tutorial/content "If we wish to find the flux through a tilted plane, we should first calculate the unit normal vector to this plane.

For example, consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle x,\: 1-x+y,\: 2y+8\rangle$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y-1$ such that $\textrm{Area}(S) = 2.$ 
Assume that we need to find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = -1, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2(1-x+y)+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2+2x-2y+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "81d0dc6b-4e76-5f80-934b-e300c50b0201" :step/math-academy-id 657086 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167788}}] :activity/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166981} {:db/id 17592186167785 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168145 :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s.
$$

The flux measures the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ as depicted below.

![](images/23/2392d6c27fc6767c78172936d6df37b3dfec8b2198abbdf9e22b87d4337ed9da.png)

Flux is always measured with respect to a preselected unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and we have two choices of orientation for this vector. If we measure the flux relative to the unit normal pointing in the *opposite* direction, our flux will have the *same* magnitude but *opposite* sign.

![](images/e4/e451548a5d9874b9eff9d61c2d423696dc76a3f560e2936eb7bdb3a9cbfbed49.png)

This lesson aims to extend the concept of flux to three-dimensional vector fields. $$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle xz + y,\: x^2,\: 2y-z^2 \right\rangle\!, 
\qquad 
\mathbf{n}(x,y,z) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\left\langle 2,\: 0,\: -1 \right\rangle\!.
$$

Let's construct a surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}.$

First, we recall that if $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}((xz+y)\cdot 2+{x}^{2}\cdot 0+(2y-{z}^{2})\cdot (-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2xz+2y-2y+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf n$ can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{∬}_{S}2xz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S\end{aligned}
$$

We can then evaluate this integral using the usual methods." :tutorial/id #uuid "c936101d-fbb9-594d-888c-2327d0908e71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7632 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "88355efb-c547-50b1-b76e-a290fd494387" :step/math-academy-id 657078 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167783}} {:db/id 17592186168144 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ where

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "81d0dc6b-4e76-5f80-934b-e300c50b0201" :step/math-academy-id 657086 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167788}} {:db/id 17592186168145 :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "15c5dca7-7c90-57e5-be91-60bf5e44e76b" :step/math-academy-id 657076 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167786}} {:db/id 17592186167786 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign.

As in the case of two-dimensional vector fields, we have a choice between two possible normal vectors at each point. For instance, we could have picked the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction, as shown below.

<div id="graphic-b46ee2d2f4637027c6704e244e0b2f96" class="graphic"><img src="/graphics/b46ee2d2f4637027c6704e244e0b2f96" /></div> 

The key takeaway is that when calculating the flux of a vector field across a surface, we must be clear about which orientation we're measuring our flux relative to." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "4b9873f3-a548-5ea9-a86b-7682d0efa06b" :step/math-academy-id 657077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167782}} {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign.

As in the case of two-dimensional vector fields, we have a choice between two possible normal vectors at each point. For instance, we could have picked the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction, as shown below.

<div id="graphic-b46ee2d2f4637027c6704e244e0b2f96" class="graphic"><img src="/graphics/b46ee2d2f4637027c6704e244e0b2f96" /></div> 

The key takeaway is that when calculating the flux of a vector field across a surface, we must be clear about which orientation we're measuring our flux relative to." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} {:db/id 17592186167788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166882 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166487 :question/id #uuid "35c3c9ba-60b0-5bcf-8e9c-2862ece44e7e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12454"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9a62365-4278-557f-ba76-caa31abe7869" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167129} {:db/id 17592186167130} {:db/id 17592186278417} {:db/id 17592186278418} {:db/id 17592186281387} {:db/id 17592186281388} {:db/id 17592186281492} {:db/id 17592186281494} {:db/id 17592186281496} {:db/id 17592186369894} {:db/id 17592186369908}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "99f84857-19d8-532f-b1f8-974d1ed142df" :step/math-academy-id 657087} {:db/id 17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter. 

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we have that

\begin{align*}
\mathbf r_x =  \langle 1, 0, 0\rangle = \mathbf i, \qquad \mathbf r_y =  \langle 0, 1, 0\rangle = \mathbf j.
\end{align*}

So, the fundamental vector product is given by

\[
\mathbf r_x \times\mathbf r_y = \mathbf i\times\mathbf j = \mathbf k
\]

and therefore

\[
|| \mathbf r_x \times\mathbf r_y|| = ||\mathbf k|| =1. 
\]

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3a45ce20-02a0-56e8-9b38-add2ba9480d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7733 :tutorial/title "The Fundamental Vector Product for a Horizontal Plane"} {:db/id 17592186362413 :tutorial/content "If we wish to find the flux through a tilted plane, we should first calculate the unit normal vector to this plane.

For example, consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle x,\: 1-x+y,\: 2y+8\rangle$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y-1$ such that $\textrm{Area}(S) = 2.$ 
Assume that we need to find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = -1, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2(1-x+y)+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2+2x-2y+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} {:db/id 17592186045463
